newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban alliance bombs Kabul in fresh assault.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban alliance bombs Kabul in fresh assault.

text.p: Forces loyal to the ousted Afghan government bombed Kabul and launched a blistering assault on Taleban troops north of the capital on Thursday, breaking a two-day lull in Afghanistan's latest war.
The assault, on both the De Sabz pass about 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul, and another pass, Khair Khana, also north of Kabul, began at around 6 a.m. (0130 GMT) on Thursday.

It was followed shortly by a bombing apparently aimed at the capital's main airport in northeastern Kabul, which killed three children and wounded seven people. Witnesses said the airport, used for both military and civilian traffic, appeared undamaged.
The deaths were believed to be the first war-related civilian fatalities in Kabul since the purist Islamic Taleban militia overtook the capital in late September.
Fierce heavy artillery and rocket duels churned up columns of dust around the strategic De Sabz pass,

"The objective is to advance as far forward as possible," Mehrabuddin Masstan, a spokesman for the commander of former government forces, Ahmad Shah Masood, told reporters at the force's headquaters in Jabal os-Siraj further north.
This correspondent saw shells and rockets pound the barren mountainside several times a minute.

Masstan said he could not confirm whether any ground had been secured by the anti-Taleban alliance, made up of Masood's troops and heavy weapons and those of the northern Uzbek leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
But he said the assault was "progressing well".
About an hour after the ground attack, warplanes believed to belong to Dostum dropped five bombs over Kabul.
One of the bombs hit a mountainside next to the airport, while two more hit a field about 400 metres (yards) from the airport, one of which failed to explode.

A further two 250 kg (550 lb) bombs landed in the Deh Kepak district in northwest Kabul around 8 a.m. (0330 GMT), killing three children and wounding seven people, witnesses said. There were no reports of injuries from the other bombs.
The Taleban militia fired one ground-to-air missile, but it did not appear to hit any of the planes.
The father of two of the dead children, Dr Abdullah, was in serious condition in hospital. His seven-year-old son Hamid and 14-year-old daughter Malina were killed, witnesses said.
"They were having breakfast when the bombs landed," said Khan Coco, a neighbour who was digging through the remains of a mud-brick house looking for survivors.

In the other house that was hit, the body of the third dead child, seven-year-old Matine, lay on a rope-strung bed covered with the blanket under which he had spent his last night. The assault on the passes is the third in nine days. The previous two attacks were stalemated around both passes, viewed by the former government as "the gates to Kabul".
A senior source in Masood's camp said retaking Kabul from the Taleban militia was both politically and militarily vital.
"We must take Kabul as this will be a sign that we are serious and other provinces will follow (revolt against the Taleban)," the source said.
A deep, baleful roar announced a clutch of rockets streaming from a large, Soviet-type "Uragan", or "Hurricane", multi-barrelled launcher from the anti-Taleban side.
Orange flashes, white smoke and deafening crashes announced return fire from the Taleban as their rockets landed on the former government's exposed positions on the mountainside below the pass.
Taleban shells also landed near the old road into Kabul, below the Khair Khana pass.
A commander on the old road said there had been fighting around the village of Hussein Kot, about 20 km (12 miles) north of Kabul.
